q: On the G1, what torque does MuJoCo's position actuator actually compute?
choices: τ = k_p(q_ref − q) − k_v·q̇, a PD law
τ = k_p(q_ref − q) + k_i∫e dt, a PI law
τ = k_p(q_ref − q) alone, a pure spring
none: it sets q = q_ref exactly each step
why: The 'position actuator' is a PD controller written into the model file: a spring toward the command plus a damper on velocity. It is not an ideal servo that teleports the joint, and it has no integral term.

q: The position actuator sits on a seam between two layers of the stack. Which?
choices: Declared in Layer 2 (robot model), doing Layer 4's (control) job
Declared in Layer 4 (control), doing Layer 1's (physics) job
Declared in Layer 5 (AI), doing Layer 4's (control) job
Declared in Layer 1 (physics), doing Layer 2's (model) job
why: The actuator is written in the MJCF (Layer 2), but what it declares is a feedback controller, which is Layer 4's job. That is why the guide calls it 'a controller in disguise'.

q: In τ = k_p(q_ref − q) − k_v·q̇, what does the D term do while the joint is moving TOWARD its target?
choices: Brakes it anyway: it opposes motion in either direction
Speeds it up, adding torque toward the target
Nothing: it acts only when moving away from the target
Reverses sign so that it helps the P term pull
why: −k_v·q̇ depends only on the velocity, not on the error, so it resists any motion, even motion toward the target. Thinking D 'helps' the joint arrive is the common slip.

q: In the spring–damper picture of the servo, what are the spring and the damper attached to?
choices: Spring to the command; damper to the ground
Spring to the ground; damper to the command
Both to the command, so both move with ctrl
Both to the ground, so neither moves with ctrl
why: Moving ctrl drags the spring's end (the P term pulls toward the command), while the damper is fixed to the ground, so it brakes all motion. Swapping them would make the damper oppose only motion relative to the command.

q: MuJoCo's general actuator is τ = g0·ctrl + b0 + b1·q + b2·q̇. Which settings make it the PD position servo?
why: Collecting terms gives k_p·ctrl − k_p·q − k_v·q̇ = k_p(ctrl − q) − k_v·q̇. So k_p appears twice (gain and bias); leaving b1 = 0 would give a torque that does not depend on q at all.

q: To make a servo stiffer you change only gainprm[0] (g0) from 500 to 1000 and leave biasprm alone. What happens?
choices: It now pulls toward a different angle than ctrl
It is twice as stiff and still pulls toward ctrl
Nothing: only biasprm sets the stiffness
The damping doubles; the stiffness is unchanged
why: k_p appears twice (g0 and b1 = −k_p). With g0 = 1000 and b1 = −500 the torque is zero at q = 2·ctrl, so the servo aims at the wrong angle. That is why scale_gains writes three numbers.

q: An actuator has g0 = 1000, b1 = −500, b0 = b2 = 0 (gravity off). With ctrl = 0.1 rad, where does the joint come to rest?
choices: q = 0.2 rad
q = 0.1 rad
q = 0.05 rad
q = 0.4 rad
why: At rest τ = 0: 1000·0.1 − 500·q = 0, so q = 100/500 = 0.2 rad. It would be 0.1 rad only if g0 and −b1 were equal, as in a real position actuator.

q: How do the G1's servo gains vary across its joints?
choices: k_p = 500 everywhere; k_v ranges about 4.55 to 43
k_v = 500 everywhere; k_p ranges about 4.55 to 43
k_p = 500 on the legs, 100 on the arms; k_v fixed
k_p ranges 250 to 1000; k_v = 15.85 everywhere
why: Stiffness is uniform (500) and damping is not: k_v spans roughly tenfold, 4.55 to 43. 15.85 is the knee's k_v alone, and 250/1000 are the sweep values that fall.

q: One servoed joint, gravity off, other joints held still. Which equation does it obey?
choices: M·q̈ + k_v·q̇ + k_p·q = k_p·q_ref
M·q̈ + k_p·q̇ + k_v·q = k_v·q_ref
M·q̇ + k_v·q = k_p·q_ref
M·q̈ = k_p·q_ref − k_v·q
why: Newton for rotation (M·q̈ = τ) with the PD torque, unknowns moved left: the mass–spring–damper equation. It is second order, with damping on q̇ and stiffness on q; the swapped version mixes up k_p and k_v.

q: In the one-joint model M·q̈ + k_v·q̇ + k_p·q = k_p·q_ref, what is M for the knee?
choices: Inertia of everything beyond the joint about its axis, plus armature
The total mass of the robot, about 33 kg, felt equally by every joint
The rotor inertia of the knee motor alone, read from its datasheet
The inertia of the bodies on the pelvis side of the knee, thigh up
why: M is the joint's diagonal entry of the mass matrix (mj_fullM): what the knee must swing (shin and foot), plus the motor's armature (0.01 kg·m² on G1 leg joints). It is not the whole robot's mass and not the bodies on the pelvis side.

q: Substituting e = e^(rt) into M·ë + k_v·ė + k_p·e = 0 gives which characteristic equation?
choices: M·r² + k_v·r + k_p = 0
k_p·r² + k_v·r + M = 0
M·r² + k_p·r + k_v = 0
r² + k_v·r + k_p·M = 0
why: Each derivative brings down one r: M·r²·e^(rt) + k_v·r·e^(rt) + k_p·e^(rt) = 0, then cancel e^(rt). The inertia goes with r², the damping with r, the stiffness alone.

q: Matching M·r² + k_v·r + k_p = 0 to r² + 2ζω_n·r + ω_n² = 0 gives which ω_n and ζ?
choices: ω_n = k_p/M, ζ = k_v/(2·k_p·M)
ω_n = √(k_p·M), ζ = k_v/√(k_p/M)
why: Divide by M: ω_n² = k_p/M and 2ζω_n = k_v/M, so ζ = k_v/(2Mω_n) = k_v/(2√(k_p·M)). Forgetting the square root or the 2 are the usual slips.

q: k_p = 400 N·m/rad, M = 1 kg·m², k_v = 40 N·m·s/rad. What are ω_n and ζ?
choices: ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 1.0
ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 2.0
ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 0.5
why: ω_n = √(400/1) = 20; ζ = 40/(2·√400) = 40/40 = 1.0, critically damped. Dropping the 2 gives ζ = 2; skipping the root gives ω_n = 400.

q: k_p = 100, M = 4 kg·m², k_v = 10. What are ω_n and ζ?
choices: ω_n = 5 rad/s, ζ = 0.25
ω_n = 5 rad/s, ζ = 0.5
why: ω_n = √(100/4) = 5; ζ = 10/(2·√400) = 10/40 = 0.25, so it rings (about 44 % overshoot). ζ = 0.5 comes from forgetting the 2; ω_n = 20 is √(k_p·M) instead of √(k_p/M).

q: Practice Q14: k_p = 900, M = 1 kg·m², k_v = 30. What are ω_n and ζ, and does it overshoot?
choices: ω_n = 30 rad/s, ζ = 0.5; yes, about 16 %
ω_n = 30 rad/s, ζ = 1.0; no overshoot
ω_n = 900 rad/s, ζ = 0.5; yes, about 16 %
ω_n = 30 rad/s, ζ = 0.5; yes, about 44 %
why: ω_n = √900 = 30; ζ = 30/(2·30) = 0.5, under-damped, overshoot exp(−π·0.5/√0.75) ≈ 16 %. 44 % belongs to ζ = 0.25; ζ = 1.0 forgets the 2.

q: k_p = 400, M = 0.25 kg·m². Which k_v makes the joint critically damped (ζ = 1)?
choices: 20 N·m·s/rad
10 N·m·s/rad
40 N·m·s/rad
100 N·m·s/rad
why: ζ = 1 means k_v = 2√(k_p·M) = 2√100 = 20. 10 forgets the 2; 100 is k_p·M without the root.

q: k_p = 200, M = 2 kg·m². Which k_v gives ζ = 1?
choices: 40 N·m·s/rad
20 N·m·s/rad
400 N·m·s/rad
10 N·m·s/rad
why: k_v = 2√(k_p·M) = 2√400 = 2·20 = 40. 20 is √(k_p·M) without the 2; 400 is k_p·M with no root; 10 would be 2√(k_p/M).

q: For ζ < 1, what are the characteristic roots and what does the joint do?
choices: A complex pair −ζω_n ± iω_d: it overshoots and rings
A double real root −ω_n: fastest arrival with no overshoot
Two different negative real roots: it creeps in slowly
A pair with positive real part: the joint diverges
why: Below ζ = 1 the square root √(ζ² − 1) is imaginary, so the roots are complex: decay times oscillation, i.e. ringing. The double root is ζ = 1 and two real roots is ζ > 1; with k_v > 0 nothing diverges.

q: What does critical damping (ζ = 1) give a joint's step response?
choices: The fastest arrival without any overshoot
The fastest arrival of any ζ, with slight overshoot
Zero steady-state sag under a gravity load
The slowest arrival, but with the least torque
why: ζ = 1 is the double root −ω_n: the quickest response that never passes the target. Lower ζ can get near the target sooner but overshoots; ζ says nothing about sag, which is τ_g/k_p.

q: An over-damped joint (ζ > 1) has two real negative roots. Which one decides how long you wait?
choices: The slow root, the one nearer zero
The fast root, the one farther from zero
Their average, which is −ζω_n
Neither: it always arrives in 1/ω_n
why: e(t) is a sum of two decaying exponentials; the fast one dies in milliseconds and the slow one is what you wait for. At ζ = 4 on the knee that slow root is −8 /s, five times slower than critical.

q: With k_v > 0 and k_p > 0, what is guaranteed about a joint's step response?
choices: It always arrives; only the way it arrives changes
It arrives only if ζ ≥ 1; below that it rings for ever
It arrives only if ζ ≤ 1; above that it stalls short
It arrives only if k_p is larger than k_v
why: With k_v > 0 both roots have negative real part, so every term decays: 'the joint always arrives; the question is how'. Ringing decays, and over-damped creeping still converges.

q: For an under-damped joint, what is the magnitude of each complex root?
choices: Exactly ω_n
Exactly ζ·ω_n
Exactly ω_d = ω_n√(1 − ζ²)
Exactly 2ζ·ω_n
why: |r|² = (ζω_n)² + ω_d² = ω_n²(ζ² + 1 − ζ²) = ω_n². So damping slides the pair around a circle of radius ω_n; ζω_n is only the real part and ω_d only the imaginary part.

q: ω_n = 10 rad/s and ζ = 0.6. What are the characteristic roots?
why: Real part −ζω_n = −6; imaginary part ω_d = ω_n√(1 − 0.36) = 10·0.8 = 8. Check: |−6 + 8i| = 10 = ω_n. Using ω_n itself as the imaginary part gives −6 ± 10i.

q: The one-joint step response's overshoot, exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)), depends on what?
choices: ζ only
ω_n only: quicker joints overshoot more
The step size: bigger steps overshoot more
k_p alone, whatever the damping
why: The formula contains nothing but ζ, so two joints with very different speeds but the same ζ overshoot by the same fraction. Stiffness changes the overshoot only through ζ.

q: What overshoot does exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) give at ζ = 0.25, 0.5 and 1?
why: ζ = 0.25 gives 44 %, ζ = 0.5 gives 16 %, and at ζ = 1 the peak time is infinite, so there is no overshoot. 56 % is the measured P-only knee, a different experiment.

q: Complete the professor's line: 'Stiffness sets the ___; the damping ratio sets the ___.'
choices: speed; shape
shape; speed
sag; speed
torque; sag
why: ω_n = √(k_p/M) sets how fast the joint responds; ζ alone sets whether it overshoots (the shape). The reversed version is the tempting misremembering.

q: A joint has ω_n = 10 rad/s and ζ = 1. You quadruple k_p, keeping M and k_v. What are the new ω_n and ζ?
choices: ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 0.5
ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 1.0
ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 2.0
why: ω_n ∝ √k_p doubles to 20, and ζ = k_v/(2√(k_p·M)) ∝ 1/√k_p halves to 0.5. Scaling linearly (×4, ÷4) or assuming ζ is unchanged are the slips.

q: A critically damped joint is made 4× stiffer (k_p × 4, k_v unchanged) to respond faster. What happens to its shape?
choices: ζ halves to 0.5, so it now overshoots (≈16 % by formula)
ζ stays 1.0, because ζ depends only on k_v and M
ζ doubles to 2, so it becomes sluggish and creeps in
ζ drops to 0.25, so it overshoots by about 44 %
why: ζ = k_v/(2√(k_p·M)) contains k_p under a root, so ×4 stiffness halves ζ. Quadrupling k_p doubles the speed AND halves ζ; to keep ζ = 1 you would have to double k_v too.

q: On the lifted G1 knee (0.5 rad step), what did k_p × 4 do compared with the shipped gains?
choices: 1 % in 0.032 s vs 0.110 s; 4 % overshoot; 1000 N·m peak
1 % in 0.220 s vs 0.110 s; no overshoot; 250 N·m peak
1 % in 0.032 s vs 0.110 s; no overshoot; 250 N·m peak
Never within 1 % in 0.5 s: it became over-damped
why: ×4 stiffness doubles ω_n and halves ζ to 0.5, so it arrives about 3.4× sooner, pays a 4.0 % overshoot, and draws 4× the torque (k_p × 0.5 rad = 1000 N·m). Over-damped is what k_p ÷ 4 does.

q: Just after a 0.5 rad step, the error is the whole step. What is the initial torque at k_p = 500, and at k_p = 2000?
choices: 250 N·m and 1000 N·m
250 N·m and 500 N·m
500 N·m and 2000 N·m
1000 N·m and 4000 N·m
why: τ = k_p·e at q̇ = 0: 500·0.5 = 250 N·m and 2000·0.5 = 1000 N·m. Torque scales linearly with k_p, not with √k_p, so a 4× stiffer servo draws 4× the torque.

q: Why does the G1's k_v vary about tenfold across the leg joints while k_p is 500 on all of them?
choices: Each leg joint is set to ζ = 1, so k_v = 2√(k_p·M) tracks M
Each leg joint is set to the same ω_n, so k_v must cancel M
k_v was hand-tuned per joint to minimise sag during the walk
Heavier joints need more stiffness, and k_v is what supplies it
why: Solving ζ = 1 for the damping gives k_v = 2√(k_p·M): same k_p, different M, different k_v. So the heavy hip and the light ankle respond with the same shape. Damping has no effect on sag.

q: What damping ratio do the G1's twelve leg joints have, and its arm joints?
choices: Legs all ζ = 1.00; arms looser, 0.7–1.9
Legs all ζ = 0.5; arms all ζ = 1.00
Legs spread 0.7–1.9; arms all ζ = 1.00
Legs all ζ = 0.25; arms all ζ = 4
why: Read M off the mass matrix and compute ζ: every leg joint is exactly critically damped, while the arms spread 0.7–1.9. The legs got the design rule; the arms did not.

q: For the G1 knee (M ≈ 0.126 kg·m², k_p = 500), what is ω_n?
choices: About 63 rad/s, roughly 10 Hz
About 4000 rad/s, roughly 630 Hz
About 10 rad/s, roughly 1.6 Hz
About 63 Hz, roughly 400 rad/s
why: √(500/0.126) ≈ √4000 ≈ 63 rad/s, and 63/(2π) ≈ 10 Hz: an undamped knee would ring ten times a second. 4000 is ω_n² (forgot the root); '63 Hz' confuses rad/s with Hz.

q: For the G1 knee, what are its basic time unit 1/ω_n and the time critical damping takes to get within 1 %?
choices: About 16 ms; about 0.1 s (≈ 6.6/ω_n)
About 0.1 s; about 0.6 s (≈ 6.6/ω_n)
About 16 ms; about 16 ms (one time unit)
About 1.6 ms; about 10 ms (≈ 6.6/ω_n)
why: 1/63 ≈ 16 ms, and (1 + x)e^(−x) = 0.01 at x ≈ 6.6, so critical damping needs about seven time units ≈ 0.105 s. It does not arrive in one time unit.

q: A critically damped joint gets within 1 % after about 6.6/ω_n. For ω_n = 20 rad/s, how long is that?
choices: About 0.33 s
About 0.05 s
About 1.05 s
About 3.0 s
why: 6.6/20 = 0.33 s. 0.05 s is one time unit 1/ω_n; 1.05 s would come from dividing by 2π instead of ω_n.

q: The knee with k_v × 4 (ζ = 4): what are its roots, and how long to reach 1 %?
choices: −8 and −497 /s; about 0.58 s, set by the slow root
−63 and −63 /s; about 0.1 s, as fast as critical
−16 ± 61i /s; about 0.03 s, with 44 % overshoot
−8 and −497 /s; about 0.02 s, set by the fast root
why: Over-damped: two real roots whose product is ω_n² (8 × 497 ≈ 63²). The fast one dies in milliseconds; the slow e^(−8t) is what you wait for, about 0.577 s.

q: On the G1 lifted clear of the floor, k_v/4 on the knee overshot 16.9 %, but the one-joint formula predicts 44 %. Why?
choices: The other joints and the floating pelvis move back; nothing is a wall
MuJoCo's integrator adds numerical damping that eats the ringing
The formula is wrong: overshoot really depends on ω_n as well
The 0.3 N·m joint friction absorbs most of the swing energy
why: The one-joint model assumes every other joint is welded still; in a floating robot the knee pushes against a body that gives way, so less inertia and relatively more damping. The formula is right about direction and design rule, only approximate in numbers.

q: What does the guide say to do with the one-joint formula on a whole robot?
choices: Use it to choose gains; measure to know what you got
Trust it over measurement, since simulation is approximate
Use it only on the arms; legs need the full mass matrix
Discard it on a humanoid and tune gains by trial alone
why: It over-predicts ringing (44 % vs 16.9 %) but its design rule (ζ = 1, no overshoot) holds. The course's thread is 'measure, do not believe', so the formula guides and the measurement decides.

q: With k_v/4 on the knee of the lifted G1, the one-joint formula predicts 44 % overshoot. What did the real robot do?
choices: Rang less, 16.9 %: the rest of the body gives way
Exactly 44 %, just as the one-joint formula predicts
Rang more, about 56 %: the pelvis adds extra inertia
No overshoot at all, since the legs are critically damped
why: The formula OVER-predicts ringing on the real robot (16.9 % measured vs 44 %), because the other joints and the floating pelvis move back. k_v/4 makes ζ = 0.25, so the joint is no longer critically damped.

q: At rest under a gravity torque τ_g, the servo balances 0 = k_p(q_ref − q) + τ_g. What is the sag?
choices: q − q_ref = τ_g/k_p
q − q_ref = τ_g·k_p
q − q_ref = τ_g/k_v
q − q_ref = τ_g/(k_p + k_v)
why: At rest q̇ = 0, so the damper contributes nothing and the spring alone holds the load: deflection = load ÷ stiffness. Damping cannot appear in it.

q: A servo with k_p = 300 N·m/rad holds a 6 N·m gravity load. How large is the steady sag?
choices: 0.02 rad
0.2 rad
0.05 rad
why: τ_g/k_p = 6/300 = 0.02 rad (about 1.1°). The sag shrinks as k_p grows; multiplying instead of dividing is the classic slip.

q: Practice Q3: k_p = 400 holds a joint against 8 N·m of gravity. What is the steady error, and what if k_p is doubled?
choices: 0.02 rad, then 0.01 rad
0.02 rad, then 0.04 rad
0.02 rad, then exactly zero
0.05 rad, then 0.025 rad
why: 8/400 = 0.02 rad; doubling k_p halves it to 0.01 rad, never zero, because a PD spring needs an error to make the holding torque.

q: Which change removes the steady gravity sag of a servo completely?
choices: Adding an integral (I) term
Raising k_p as high as possible
Raising k_v until it is over-damped
Setting the damping ratio to exactly 1
why: Only the I term remembers the past and keeps growing until the error is zero; on the knee it ended up carrying the whole 10 N·m. A finite k_p only shrinks the sag, and damping changes how it arrives, not where.

q: 'With a stiff enough PD servo, the sag goes to zero.' Why is this wrong?
choices: Sag is τ_g/k_p: halved by doubling k_p, but never zero
Sag is τ_g/k_v: only the damper sets it, not k_p
Sag grows with k_p, since a stiffer spring takes more load
Sag is fixed by ζ, so stiffness changes the shape only
why: The error is what produces the holding torque, so a finite spring must deflect. 'A spring at rest is a spring under load, and load means deflection.'

q: 'A spring at rest is a spring under load, and load means deflection.' What does this line explain?
choices: Why a PD servo holding a weight sits off its command
Why a joint overshoots when its damping is too low
Why the hand-written servo blows up at 500 Hz
Why the CPG falls despite a plausible step pattern
why: The servo is a spring, and a spring only pushes when stretched; holding gravity therefore needs a steady error τ_g/k_p. That is the sag, not ringing or numerical instability.

q: How much steady pelvis sag does the whole walking G1 have at k_p = 500?
choices: About 11 mm
About 11 cm
About 0.11 mm
Exactly zero
why: Each leg joint sags by its own τ_g/k_p and those small angles add up along the leg to about 11 mm. Not a bug: the necessary deflection of finite springs holding up a 33 kg robot.

q: The G1's arm held straight out loads its shoulder with 4.7 N·m at k_p = 500. How much does it sag?
choices: About 9.5 mrad, half a degree
About 95 mrad, over 5 degrees
About 0.95 mrad, a twentieth of a degree
About 20 mrad, over a degree
why: 4.7/500 ≈ 9.4 mrad, and the measured 9.5 mrad lands on τ_g/k_p within 0.05 mrad (about 3.6 mm at the wrist). 20 mrad is the knee experiment's 10 N·m load.

q: The G1's joints have frictionloss 0.3 N·m. What does that do to the sag at k_p = 500?
choices: A dead band: rest may be up to 0.6 mrad either side of τ_g/k_p
It removes the sag, since friction holds the load instead
It doubles the sag, since friction adds to the gravity torque
Nothing: friction acts only when the joint moves fast
why: Friction can hold up to 0.3 N·m either way, so the spring may rest anywhere within ±0.3/k_p = ±0.6 mrad of the prediction. It neither removes nor doubles the sag.

q: In τ = k_p·e + k_i∫e dt + k_d·ė, which term reacts to what?
choices: P to the present, I to the past, D to the trend
P to the past, I to the trend, D to the present
P to the trend, I to the present, D to the past
P to the present, I to the trend, D to the past
why: P uses the error now, I accumulates error over time (it remembers), D uses how fast the error changes (it brakes before the target).

q: One knee, 0.5 rad step, 10 N·m load: rise time and overshoot of P vs PD?
choices: P 19 ms, 56 % overshoot; PD 78 ms, 0 %
P 78 ms, 0 %; PD 19 ms, 56 % overshoot
P 72 ms, 57 % overshoot; PD 19 ms, 16 %
why: P is quick (19 ms) only because it rings (56 %); PD brakes (0 %) and is slower (78 ms). The swapped pair is what the textbook table leads you to expect.

q: Same knee test: final error of P, PD, PI and PID?
why: P and PD keep the full sag 10/500 = 20 mrad; only the laws with an I term head toward zero (1.7 and 0.8 mrad after 4 s). Adding D does not move the final value.

q: The textbook table calls PD 'fast'. On the G1 knee, which rose faster, and why?
choices: P (19 vs 78 ms): it is quick only because it rings
PD (19 vs 78 ms): the D term speeds the arrival
Neither: D changes the overshoot, not the rise
PD, because D removes the sag that slows P down
why: Measured, PD rose SLOWER than P. P is under-damped, so it races past the target: 'the quickness is the ringing'. D is a brake, and it never removes sag.

q: Adding a D term to a P servo on the loaded knee changes the final error from 20 mrad to what?
choices: 20 mrad: D changes how it arrives, not where
0 mrad: the D term removes the steady error
10 mrad: the D term halves the steady error
40 mrad: the D term adds to the gravity sag
why: At rest q̇ = 0, so the D term is zero and the spring alone holds the load at τ_g/k_p = 20 mrad. D only shapes the approach (0 % overshoot instead of 56 %).

q: In the PID knee run, who carries the 10 N·m load after 4 s?
choices: The I term, about 9.6 N·m; P is down to 0.4 N·m
The P term, 10 N·m, at a 20 mrad error
The D term, since the joint still creeps slowly
P and D equally, about 5 N·m each
why: The integral has 'remembered' the sag and supplies almost all the holding torque, so P needs almost no error. In PD there is no memory, so P must keep 10 N·m and therefore 20 mrad of error for ever.

q: What does the I term cost, as seen in PI on the knee?
choices: Ringing and slow settling: 57 % overshoot, 1.0 s to 2 %
Extra sag: the final error grows from 20 to 40 mrad
Nothing: PI matched PID in every column of the table
Rise time only: it rises in 78 ms instead of 19 ms
why: The integral keeps pushing after the error crosses zero, so PI overshoots as much as P and settles slowly. PID tames it with D: 0 % overshoot, inside 2 % after 0.17 s.

q: Which member of the family is the G1's servo (MuJoCo's position actuator)?
choices: PD: it has no integral term, so it sags
PID: the I term sits in biasprm[0]
PI: the joint friction supplies the damping
P: k_v is only the joint's passive damping
why: τ = g0·ctrl + b0 + b1·q + b2·q̇ has nothing that integrates the past, so it is PD, and that is why the robot sags. b0 is a constant offset, not an integral.

q: With a torque limit, τ = clip(k_p·e − k_v·q̇, −τmax, τmax). At rest, the law stays linear only while…
choices: |e| ≤ τmax/k_p
|e| ≤ k_p/τmax
|e| ≤ τmax·k_p
|e| ≤ τmax/k_v
why: At rest the torque is k_p·e, which stays inside the clip while |k_p·e| ≤ τmax. Beyond that band the torque is stuck at the limit.

q: Practice Q15: a motor's limit is 30 N·m and k_p = 600. Over what error range is the servo linear?
choices: |e| ≤ 20 rad
|e| ≤ 0.5 rad
why: τmax/k_p = 30/600 = 0.05 rad (about 2.9°). 20 rad is k_p/τmax, the inverted ratio.

q: With a 50 N·m limit and k_p = 500, how wide is the saturation band?
choices: 0.1 rad, about 5.7°
0.1 rad, about 0.1°
10 rad, about 573°
0.01 rad, about 0.57°
why: 50/500 = 0.1 rad, and 0.1 rad × 57.3 °/rad ≈ 5.7°. Outside ±5.7° of error the knee stops being a spring.

q: Outside the saturation band, what is the servo's effective stiffness?
choices: Zero: more error buys no more torque
Still k_p: torque keeps growing with error
Doubled: the motor switches to a high-gain mode
Negative: torque reverses to protect the motor
why: Once k_p·e exceeds τmax the output is stuck at τmax, so extra bending meets no extra torque. Everything derived before (ω_n, ζ, sag) assumed the linear band.

q: Gravity asks a joint for 8 N·m but its motor saturates at 6 N·m. What makes it hold?
choices: No k_p will: it gives way until the load falls to 6 N·m
Doubling k_p, so the servo pushes twice as hard
Raising k_v, so the joint resists the falling motion
Setting ζ = 1, so it settles without any overshoot
why: Past saturation the torque is τmax whatever k_p is; an arm, for example, sinks until its lever arm is short enough that gravity's torque has dropped to the limit. Stiffness never enters.

q: What torque limits do the G1's motors have in the shipped MJCF model?
choices: None: the model limits the commanded angle, not the torque
50 N·m on every joint, matching the real G1's motors
124 N·m, which is the walker's measured peak torque
k_p × 1 rad = 500 N·m, set by the servo stiffness
why: The motors in the model are infinitely strong: ctrlrange clips the commanded angle to the joint range, but nothing bounds the torque. 124 N·m is what the walker drew, and nothing objected.

q: What peak torque did the week-4 walker draw in the unlimited model?
choices: About 124 N·m
About 12 N·m
About 50 N·m
About 1000 N·m
why: The walker peaked at about 124 N·m (at landing from its start pose) and nothing objected. 50 N·m is the limit at which it falls; 1000 N·m was the ×4-stiff step.

q: With a torque limit added to every motor, where is the walking threshold?
choices: 50 N·m falls, 55 N·m walks
124 N·m falls, 150 N·m walks
25 N·m falls, 30 N·m walks
5 N·m falls, 6 N·m walks
why: A crisp threshold: the gait needs more than 50 N·m and survives at 55. 6 N·m is the weak-shoulder arm experiment, not the walk.

q: With a 50 N·m limit, how much of the walk does the knee spend above 50 N·m, and with what result?
choices: About 4 %, and that is enough to drop the robot
About 40 %, so the fall is no surprise
About 4 %, too little to matter; it walks fine
None; the fall comes from the hip instead
why: The knee exceeds 50 N·m only at support exchanges, about 4 % of the walk, but in those moments it is outside its linear band and has zero effective stiffness, so the robot goes down.

q: Why is the missing torque limit called a sim-to-real gap 'in plain sight'?
choices: No real motor is unbounded, and closing it costs one line in the model
Real motors are stronger than the model's, so sim under-uses them
The limit is hidden in MuJoCo's C code, where students cannot see it
Real motors are limited in angle only, exactly like the model's
why: Every real actuator has a stall torque, thermal limit and gearbox; the model has none, which is visible right in the MJCF and fixable with one attribute. The direction is: sim is too strong, not too weak.

q: Scaling every k_p on the walker to 250, 500 or 1000: which walk?
choices: Only 500; 250 collapses and 1000 throws it over
All three walk; only the amount of sag changes
500 and 1000 walk; only the soft 250 collapses
Only 1000 walks; the stiffest servo tracks best
why: Only the nominal gain walks: halve it and the legs collapse, double it and the servos overpower the gait's timing. Stiffer is not simply better.

q: If k_v is rescaled to keep ζ = 1 at k_p = 250 and k_p = 1000, does the walker survive?
choices: No: ζ keeps the shape, but the speed and sag the gait was tuned for change
Yes: ζ = 1 is the only thing the walking gait needs from the servos
Only at 1000: a stiffer servo with ζ = 1 is better in every respect
No: ζ = 1 cannot be reached at those k_p values with positive k_v
why: Holding ζ fixes the shape, but ω_n ∝ √k_p and sag ∝ 1/k_p still change, and the gait's timing was tuned against this one plant. Still only the nominal gain survives.

q: Two CPG legs: φ̇_L = ω_L + w·sin(φ_R − φ_L − π), and symmetrically for R. The phase error e = φ_R − φ_L − π obeys…
choices: ė = (ω_R − ω_L) − 2w·sin e
ė = (ω_R − ω_L) − w·sin e
ė = (ω_R + ω_L) − 2w·cos e
ė = −2w·(ω_R − ω_L)·e
why: Subtracting the two phase equations, each leg's coupling term contributes −w·sin e, giving the factor 2. The rates enter as a difference, not a sum.

q: With equal stepping rates, what do the coupled CPG legs settle into?
choices: Anti-phase, with e → 0 as e^(−2wt)
In phase (a hop), with e → π as e^(−wt)
Anti-phase, with e falling linearly at 2w
No fixed relation: they drift for ever
why: ė = −2w·sin e ≈ −2w·e near 0, so the error decays exponentially and the legs lock half a stride apart. e = π (a hop) is also a rest point, but an unstable one.

q: Two CPG legs have unequal rates, Δω = ω_R − ω_L. When do they lock?
choices: Only if |Δω| ≤ 2w; then with a small constant lag
Only if |Δω| ≤ w/2; then exactly in anti-phase
Always, for any w > 0, given enough time
Never: unequal rates always drift apart
why: Locking needs ė = 0, i.e. sin e* = Δω/(2w), which has a solution only if |Δω| ≤ 2w. Then the faster leg is held back with a small lag e*; weaker coupling drifts for ever.

q: Two CPG legs differ in rate by Δω = 2 rad/s. What is the weakest coupling w that still locks them?
choices: w = 1 /s
w = 2 /s
w = 4 /s
why: Lock condition |Δω| ≤ 2w, so w ≥ 2/2 = 1 /s. Using |Δω| ≤ w would wrongly demand 2 /s.

q: Δω = 0.6 rad/s and coupling w = 0.2 /s. What do the two legs do?
choices: Drift apart for ever, since 2w = 0.4 < 0.6
Lock with a small lag, since any w > 0 locks
Lock exactly in anti-phase after about 1/(2w)
Lock in phase (a hop), the other rest point
why: Locking needs |Δω| ≤ 2w; here 2w = 0.4 rad/s is less than 0.6, so sin e* = 1.5 has no solution and the error wraps round and round.

q: Equal rates, coupling w = 5 /s. The anti-phase error shrinks by a factor e ≈ 2.72 every…
why: e(t) = e0·e^(−2wt), so the time constant is 1/(2w) = 1/10 = 0.1 s. 0.2 s forgets the 2.

q: The CPG was run at nine frequency × amplitude settings for 8 s each. What happened?
choices: All nine fell within about 2–3 s
All nine walked but drifted sideways
Three walked: the slowest rate at each amplitude
All nine fell within about 0.2–0.3 s
why: Every setting produced a good-looking stepping pattern and every one fell, 1.9–3.2 s in, because nothing in the CPG reasons about balance.

q: A CPG produces a perfectly plausible stepping pattern. Why does the robot still fall?
choices: Rhythm is not balance: nothing keeps the CoM over the support polygon
Its legs drift out of anti-phase unless the coupling w is very strong
Its stepping rate is faster than the servos' natural frequency ω_n
Its joint targets ask the knee for more than the 50 N·m torque limit
why: The CPG 'has no idea where the floor is': it is a clock, with no model of the CoM. That is week 4's LIPM value stated negatively. The model has no torque limit, and the package CPG runs locked phases.

q: 'An open-loop oscillator is a CPG with its spinal cord cut off from its body.' What do biological CPGs have that ours lacks?
choices: Sensory feedback that entrains the rhythm step by step
Stronger coupling between the left and right oscillators
A faster stepping frequency matched to the muscles
A balance model of the floor, planned before each step
why: Real CPGs are continuously entrained by load, joint-angle and skin feedback through reflexes: one more term in φ̇. Ours reads no sensor at all, so it is open loop.

q: What do the week-4 LIPM walker and the week-5 CPG have in common?
choices: Both are open loop: neither reads a single sensor
Both read the IMU to keep the CoM over the feet
Both walk about 1 m before they eventually fall
Both are closed loop, since their PD servos use feedback
why: Neither controller looks at the robot: one follows a precomputed plan, the other a timer. One walks because a human did the balance reasoning in advance; the CPG does not walk. Every later week closes that loop.

q: The PD law written by hand through qfrc_applied, compared with MuJoCo's own actuator, at 500 Hz?
choices: Hand-written blows up at 500 Hz, fine at 1 kHz; MuJoCo's survives 500 Hz
Both blow up at 500 Hz, and both need 1 kHz before the robot can walk
Hand-written is fine at 500 Hz, while MuJoCo's own one needs 1 kHz
Both walk at 500 Hz, so the smaller timestep is never actually needed
why: An explicit spring this stiff is unstable at dt = 0.002 (BADQACC after a few steps) and fine at 1 kHz. MuJoCo's actuator survives 500 Hz because the engine treats it implicitly.

q: Why does MuJoCo's own position actuator survive a 500 Hz timestep when the hand-written law does not?
choices: The engine treats the actuator's spring and damper implicitly
It clips the torque at 50 N·m, which keeps the step stable
It uses a smaller internal k_p than the hand-written law
It runs its own control loop at 10 kHz inside each step
why: Same law, different integration: MuJoCo folds the actuator's stiffness and damping into the implicit update, while qfrc_applied is an explicit force computed from the old state. The model has no torque limit.

q: The package CPG sets θ_knee = A_k·max(0, sin φ) while the hip uses A_h·sin φ. Why the max(0, ·)?
choices: A knee cannot bend backward, so the negative half is cut
It removes the hop, the unstable rest point at e = π
It keeps the knee torque below the 50 N·m limit
It makes the two legs lock into anti-phase faster
why: The knee bends only on the forward half of the cycle; max(0, ·) drops the half that would ask for backward bending. The anti-phase comes from φ_R = φ_L + π, not from the knee shape.
